title: Control Resonant 总监阐述为何应避免过度的「黄色油漆」引导
content:
Avoiding yellow paint was a conscious choice in Control Resonant
Design
PC
Console
News
Control Resonant director lays out case for avoiding excessive 'yellow paint'
'It has to feel like it’s on you to make a decision on what to do with those elements that you see within the world.'
Bryant Francis
,
Senior Editor
,
GameDeveloper.com
September 29, 2026
schedule
4 Min Read
Image via Remedy Entertainment
Remedy Entertainment's
Control Resonant
has finally launched to rave reviews from players and critics alike, cementing the studio's continued bona fides for producing otherworldly and unusual single-player games that attract a loyal audience. And now that the dust has settled after launch, developers have an opportunity to study the game's success—with some helpful guidance from the game's developers.
Interested readers can find some of that guidance over on the
Dropping Frames podcast
(via
Kotaku
). In the episode, director Mikael Kasurinen lays out some of the deliberate choices on concepts like the game's level design, which was a particularly complex challenge for Remedy as it expanded the game environment from the interiors of The Oldest House to the Pattern-warped streets of Manhattan in New York City, where "up" and "down" no longer have fixed definitions.
One particular level design technique Kasurinen zeroed in on was the team's approach to signposting, and specifically the decision to avoid "yellow paint," a common visual indicator that helps players navigate detailed game environments.
Related:
Paradox Interactive's Afterworld wants to entice new players to grand strategy with tasty RPG hooks
In
Control Resonant
, players navigate an open-world Manhattan through running, flying, and changing gravity to access orthogonally-adjusted areas. Kasurinen himself said this kind of design risked making the game "impenetrable," but said it was "a conscious choice" to not rely on yellow-colored visual markers, which have become common in games of similar scope and scale.
What anchored that choice, he said, was a desire for players to help players feel like they were the ones figuring out how to explore Manhattan. He feels that excessive signposting through yellow paint or other signifiers risks leaving them feeling like the game decided their path for them.
"If it feels like it’s like 'go here,' it’s not anymore a decision for the player. Somebody already decided for you," he said, adding that there's "nothing better" than feeling like they found their own way from point A to point B.
It's worth noting that this version of Manhattan isn't meant to be inscrutable. Kasurinen explained to Game Developer
earlier this year
that certain techniques—like maintaining a consistent point of gravity that guides the effects of rain and wind—help players stay oriented in this otherworldly realm. These and other techniques are what effectively replace the signposting found in other big budget games.
For developers still stressed about the possibility of players becoming frustrated and abandoning the game, it's worth looking at the bigger picture of signposting in a game like
Control Resonant
. The Control series is a horror-inspired action franchise where players are investigating and fighting to survive in environments that brush up against the edge of unknowable reality.
Related:
Warlock's magic system was built on game-bending player choices
The need to understand and interpret that reality is baked into every element of both titles, and signposting techniques run the risk of interfering with that player experience—that feeling of "I figured it out" that Kasurinen described.
Why is 'yellow paint' becoming a controversial design decision?
Remedy's choice to not use yellow-colored signposting was likely in the works before certain content creators and journalists began criticizing the practice (Kasurinen previously told Game Developer the game has been in active development for "two to three years" following four years of pre-production). But it's launching in the midst of an
unusually specific
type of backlash with players expressing frustration over a level design technique meant to make them less frustrated.
Stories on the topic have prompted developers to come forward with candid explanations for why the technique works well in certain games—and point out that even if they would prefer not to use yellow paint, its deployment in other games means certain players have come to expect and rely on its presence to understand where to go.
Related:
How you (yes, you) can benefit from 1-on-1 synchronous playtesting
One of the best explanations of this phenomenon comes from UI designer
Edd Coates
in a
2024 IGN video
(which takes something of a hyperbolic approach to discussing the yellow paint phenomenon). He told IGN that he's seen the industry widely adopt a "language" around yellow paint that is now so common, players are likely to see it and think "I can climb that," and if they don't see yellow paint they may think "I can't climb that."
"There are upsides and downsides—if you give people too much information it's handholding, if you take away the information it becomes [too] difficult. The key thing is to make sure it makes sense in the narrative."
That information adds extra weight to Remedy's decision to avoid the practice, as it means players weren't just operating in the game's friction, but against their experiences from other games as well.
Developers assessing if "yellow paint" works well for them can again turn to Kasurinen's conversation with Dropping Frames as an example of approaching the question through examining what experience you want players to have, rather than an arbitrary decision. The director said that his goal was to have players ask "did I make the right choice?" when thinking about their time with the game.
"I want people to think like that," he elaborated. "I want them doubt [themselves], go back, check again, see what they could do differently, because that’s life. That’s what m
